story: Mount Fuji (富士山) is a young volcano and an unfinished one. Layer on layer of lava and ash have built a cone 3,776 metres high. Lava flows dammed the rivers at its northern foot to make the Fuji Five Lakes. Between 864 and 866 the Jōgan eruption poured lava from the north-west flank into a lake called Senoumi, leaving two fragments of it, Saiko and Shōjiko, and the lava plain where the forest of Aokigahara now grows. The last eruption, in 1707, blew open the Hōei crater on the south-east flank and dropped ash on Edo, about 100 km away.

The rest of the park is volcanic too. Hakone is a complex volcano whose caldera is about 8 km across from east to west; about 3,000 years ago an eruption at its centre left the steaming valley of Ōwakudani and the landslides that dammed Lake Ashi. The Izu Peninsula came from the south. It began as volcanic islands on the Philippine Sea Plate, which carried them north into Honshu until they joined it as a peninsula about 600,000 years ago. Volcanoes kept growing after the collision — lava from Ōmuroyama built the Jōgasaki Coast some 4,000 years ago — and the Izu Islands to the south-east are still active.

Height and the sea give the park its range. On Fuji, dense woodland on the lower slopes gives way to conifers up to about the sixth station, then to bare volcanic gravel at the top. In Hakone's caldera, the marsh plants of Sengokuhara are a national natural monument, and the pampas-grass slope above them is kept open by burning each March. The Amagi range at the heart of Izu holds a large stand of natural beech forest. Offshore, the islands are home to the Izu thrush and Iijima's leaf warbler; table corals grow off Miyakejima, and wild Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins live around Mikurajima and Toshima.

Fuji has been sacred for as long as there are records. Shrines at its foot were built to calm the mountain's deity, and the summit above the eighth station is still the precinct of Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha. In the Edo period, pilgrim confraternities called Fuji-kō climbed it in great numbers; women were barred from the summit until 1872. Fuji and Hakone became a national park in 1936, the Izu Peninsula joined in 1955 and the Izu Islands in 1964. In 2013 Fuji was inscribed as a World Heritage cultural site, 'Fujisan, sacred place and source of artistic inspiration'.
howItWorks: Like every Japanese national park, Fuji-Hakone-Izu is a zoned regional park, not a fenced reserve. The Ministry of the Environment administers it but owns little of it: of its 121,755 hectares of land, about 18 per cent is national land, 30 per cent belongs to prefectures and towns, and just over half is private. Parts of 36 cities, towns and villages in Tokyo, Kanagawa, Yamanashi and Shizuoka lie inside it, along with the hot-spring resorts of Hakone and the Izu coast, the lakeside towns of the Fuji Five Lakes, farms, shrines and eight inhabited Izu islands. Fuji's summit above the eighth station belongs to Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha.

What you may do depends on the zone. About 6 per cent of the land is special protection zone, Fuji above its fifth stations among it: there, picking plants, catching insects, taking or moving stones, pitching a tent and lighting a fire are all prohibited by law. Two-thirds is special zone in three grades, where building, felling and similar works need a permit, and the remaining quarter is ordinary zone, where only large works must be notified. Driving off the roads is banned across 7,489 hectares of Fuji and along stretches of shore at Lakes Motosu and Saiko, and four marine park zones protect the sea floor off Ōshima, Shikinejima, Kōzushima and Miyakejima.

Other designations overlap the park. Fuji and a set of shrines, lakes and springs around it make up the World Heritage site; the Izu Peninsula has been a UNESCO Global Geopark since 2018, and Hakone a Japanese Geopark since 2012. Climbing Fuji is run by the two prefectures that share it — Yamanashi on the Yoshida Trail, Shizuoka on the Fujinomiya, Gotemba and Subashiri trails — each with its own registration, rules and fee, and both close the trails outside the summer season.

sightNotes.poi-jp-fuji-hakone-izu-mount-fuji: Japan's highest mountain at 3,776 m, last in eruption in 1707. Four trails climb from the fifth stations in a season of about ten weeks each summer.
sightNotes.poi-jp-fuji-hakone-izu-owakudani: A valley of steaming vents left by an eruption about 3,000 years ago, crossed by the Hakone Ropeway. Access depends on volcanic activity and gas.
sightNotes.poi-jp-fuji-hakone-izu-lake-ashi: Hakone's caldera lake, crossed by sightseeing boats, with Hakone Shrine and the old Tōkaidō highway at Moto-Hakone on its south-east shore.
sightNotes.poi-jp-fuji-hakone-izu-lake-motosu: The deepest of the Fuji Five Lakes. Its reflected view of Fuji is the one printed on the back of the ¥1,000 note issued from 2004.
sightNotes.poi-jp-fuji-hakone-izu-aokigahara-and-fu: Forest grown on the lava of the 864 Jōgan eruption. Fugaku Fuketsu, a lava tube in the forest, stays around 3°C in midsummer.
sightNotes.poi-jp-fuji-hakone-izu-shiraito-falls: Groundwater from Fuji spills from between lava layers in hundreds of threads down a curved cliff about 20 m high. Part of the World Heritage site.
sightNotes.poi-jp-fuji-hakone-izu-jogasaki-coast: About 9 km of black lava cliffs, left when Ōmuroyama's lava ran into the sea some 4,000 years ago.
sightNotes.poi-jp-fuji-hakone-izu-mount-mihara-izu-: Izu Ōshima's active volcano, watched around the clock by the Japan Meteorological Agency. Its 1986 eruption sent about 11,000 islanders off the island for a month.

Fujinomiya, Subashiri and Gotemba fifth stations on Fuji's south and east sides, by bus in the climbing season
Hakone-Yumoto and Odawara, the rail gateways to Hakone

planYourVisit.reservations: Mount Fuji's trails open only in the summer climbing season, from early July to 10 September, and both prefectures run their own entry system — check before you go. On the Yoshida Trail, Yamanashi Prefecture takes bookings and the fee online through its Yoshida Trail access reservation system, or on the day at the fifth-station gate; the gate closes from 14:00 to 03:00 to anyone without a mountain-hut booking, and once 4,000 climbers have passed in a day. On the Fujinomiya, Gotemba and Subashiri trails, Shizuoka Prefecture requires pre-registration in its FUJI NAVI app, including a short online course on rules and safety, and a hut booking for anyone starting between 14:00 and 03:00; registration can also be done at the trailhead. Book mountain huts well ahead for summer weekends.
permits: Mount Fuji — ¥4,000 per person per climb on every trail in the climbing season, paid to the prefecture (see Fees)
Yoshida Trail — equipment check at the fifth-station gate: climbers without warm clothing, a separate rain jacket and trousers, and proper boots are turned back
camping: No camping on Fuji's climbing routes: climbers stay in mountain huts
Lakeside campgrounds at Lake Tanuki and Lake Saiko, among others around the Fuji Five Lakes
lodging: Mountain huts on all four Fuji trails, open in the climbing season; reserve directly and early
Hotels and inns around Lake Kawaguchi and the other Fuji Five Lakes
Hot-spring inns throughout Hakone and along the Izu coast
Inns and guesthouses on the inhabited Izu Islands
seasonalClosures: All four trails to Fuji's summit close outside the climbing season. In 2026 the Yoshida and Subashiri trails opened on 1 July, the Fujinomiya and Gotemba trails on 10 July, and all closed on 10 September; check the dates for your year before you go

The Shizuoka-side roads to the Fujinomiya, Subashiri and Gotemba fifth stations close in winter (in 2026 they opened on 24 April), and private cars are barred from the Fuji Skyline, Fuji Azami Line and Fuji Subaru Line for most of the climbing season — use the shuttle buses

chronology.text: Ōmuroyama erupts on the Izu Peninsula; its lava runs into the sea to form the Jōgasaki Coast.
An eruption in the Hakone caldera opens Ōwakudani, and landslides dam Lake Ashi.
The Jōgan eruption buries the lake of Senoumi, leaving Saiko and Shōjiko, and lays the lava on which Aokigahara grows.
The Hōei eruption, Fuji's most recent, opens a crater on the south-east flank and drops ash on Edo.
Fuji-Hakone National Park is designated on 1 February.
The Izu Peninsula is added and the park becomes Fuji-Hakone-Izu.
The Izu Islands, a quasi-national park since 1955, are added to the park.
Fuji is inscribed on the World Heritage List as 'Fujisan, sacred place and source of artistic inspiration'.
Yamanashi puts a gate, a daily limit of 4,000 climbers and a ¥2,000 fee on the Yoshida Trail.
Shizuoka charges ¥4,000 on its three trails for the first time, and Yamanashi doubles its fee to match.

safety: Fuji's summit is 3,776 m. Altitude sickness — headache, nausea, dizziness — is common, and worst among people who climb through the night without sleep ('bullet climbing'), which both prefectures warn against. Stay a night in a hut, climb slowly and turn back if symptoms worsen.

Fuji, Hakone and the Izu Islands volcanoes, among them Izu-Ōshima and Miyakejima, are watched by the Japan Meteorological Agency, which sets a volcanic alert level for each: 1 means stay aware of an active volcano, 2 closes the area around the crater, 3 restricts entry to the mountain, and 4 and 5 mean evacuation. Check JMA's current level and any local closures before you go.

Ōwakudani's vents give off volcanic gas. In 2015 rising activity and a very small eruption closed the valley for more than a year. The nature trail among the vents reopened in 2022 only for escorted groups booked in advance, and it shuts when gas levels or the weather are bad. Elsewhere, keep to the open areas and follow on-site instructions.

Out of season Fuji is a winter mountain: the huts and first-aid stations are shut, mobile coverage is patchy, and snow, ice and storm-force wind make falls and exposure likely. Climbing then is strongly discouraged.
In summer, afternoon thunderstorms build quickly on Fuji, and loose rock falls on crowded upper slopes. Carry rain gear and warm clothing, and consider a helmet.
regulations: Fuji above the fifth stations is special protection zone: do not pick plants, collect insects, take or move stones, or leave the trail. Tents and fires are not allowed on the climbing routes.
Carry all rubbish home. There are no bins on Fuji's trails or at the huts, and trail and hut toilets ask a tip of about ¥100–300, so carry coins.
The landowner bans drones and paragliders above the 8.5th station, and the official climbing guidance asks climbers not to bring pets and to use stoves away from huts and crowds.
Driving off the roads is banned in designated areas on Fuji and along the shores of Lakes Motosu and Saiko.

weather: The park spans more than 3,700 metres of height and a long run of ocean, so the weather depends on where you stand. Kawaguchiko, at Fuji's northern foot, averages about 0°C in January and 22°C in August, with nearly 1,600 mm of rain a year; September and October are the wettest months. On the summit the August average is about 6°C and the January average −18°C; even in the climbing season the temperature can fall below freezing before dawn, wind adds to the chill, and afternoon thunderstorms build quickly. Izu Ōshima is mild, about 7.5°C in January and 26°C in August, but wet, with close to 2,900 mm of rain a year and October the wettest month.
directions: For the Fuji Five Lakes, highway buses run from Shinjuku and other Tokyo terminals to Kawaguchiko in a little over two hours, and limited-express trains run from Shinjuku to Kawaguchiko Station on the Fujikyu line; local buses go on to the other lakes, and in the climbing season to the fifth stations. From Shin-Fuji on the Tōkaidō Shinkansen, buses serve Shiraito Falls and the Fujinomiya trailhead. For Hakone, the Odakyu Romancecar runs from Shinjuku to Hakone-Yumoto in about 80 minutes, and the Hakone Tozan Railway climbs from Odawara; ropeways and boats cross the caldera. The Izu Peninsula is reached by the Shinkansen to Atami or Mishima, or the Odoriko limited express, with the Izukyu line south of Itō and the Izuhakone Railway to Shuzenji. Tōkai Kisen ships sail to the Izu Islands from Takeshiba Pier in Tokyo and from Atami, Shinshin Kisen's ferry from Shimoda, and there are flights from Haneda to Hachijōjima.
